reconcile.connective: Defenders distinguish two kinds of high places — Asa razed the idolatrous ones but left standing the unlawful altars to Yahweh, so both reports stand.

discrepancy.connective: C. Dennis McKinsey presses the conflict as unresolved, noting that Chronicles itself both removes the high places (14:3-5) and reports them still standing (15:17), with the 'out of Israel' qualifier read as a later softening of the clash.

skeptic.name: C. Dennis McKinsey
skeptic.attribution: C. Dennis McKinsey (d. 2009), The Encyclopedia of Biblical Errancy (Prometheus Books, 1995)

excerpts.excerpt_text: All public objects and relics of idolatry in Jerusalem and other cities through his kingdom were destroyed; but those high places where God was worshipped under the figure of an ox, as at Beth-el, were allowed to remain (Kg1 15:14); so far the reformation was incomplete.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the Asa high-places clash by distinguishing destroyed idolatrous high places from tolerated Yahweh high places, and concedes the reform was incomplete — the strongest single reconcile.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on 2 Chronicles 15:17
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this passage directly: Asa 'had totally suppressed or destroyed the idolatry; but some of the places, buildings, or altars, he permitted to remain' — the harmonizing distinction keyed to the Asa high-places difficulty.
